title: ICYMI: During Climate Week, Governor Hochul Announces Design Award for Major Resilience Project to Protect Metro-North Railroad’s Hudson Line from Effects of Climate Change

blocks.text: Part of $800 Million Project will Protect Metro-North Hudson Line from Extreme Weather Events
Project to Focus on 20-Mile Stretch from Riverdale to Croton-Harmon
Photos and Video of Today’s Announcement Available Here and Here

During NYC Climate Week, Governor Kathy Hochul today announced the Metropolitan Transportation Authority (MTA) awarded a $19.7 million contract for the design phase of a major project to protect vulnerable portions of the Metro-North Railroad’s Hudson Line from the effects of climate change and fortify the line against future stormwater runoff, tidal floods and other risks between Spuyten Duyvil to Hastings-on-Hudson. This milestone is a major step forward in a flagship $800 million resiliency effort to fortify the Hudson Line in the MTA’s 2025-2029 Capital Plan.     “The impacts of climate change and extreme weather put the commutes of millions of riders who rely on the Hudson Line each year at risk,” Governor Hochul said . “That's why we're making historic investments to ensure the long-term resilience of this vital rail corridor, fortifying it for the long term and ensuring that service is more reliable than ever before."     MTA Chair and CEO Janno Lieber said , “As I always say, mass transit is the antidote to climate change — but we need to deal with the accelerating impacts it is already having on our system. This project takes a comprehensive approach towards protecting essential Metro-North service for decades to come.”     MTA Construction & Development President Jamie Torres Springer said , "Millions of New Yorkers rely on the Hudson Line every year, but the future of the line depends on us taking action now. This design award marks a major milestone in our effort to protect our system from the effects of climate change and to safeguard the reliable transit service our region depends on."     MTA Metro-North Railroad President Justin Vonashek said , “We have a responsibility to protect this corridor and the people who depend on it every day. We are meeting that responsibility through careful planning, sustained investment, and a series of projects designed to strengthen and safeguard the Hudson Line for the long term.”     The $270 million project is targeting assets that manage water flow and drainage, stabilize the right of way, and are in poor condition along a segment of the lower Hudson that is highly vulnerable to extreme weather. Work includes the fortification of retaining walls and slopes, expansion of culverts and drainage along slopes and track, shoreline structure rehabilitation, as well as flood protection measures for tracks where possible. This project will also develop a resilient design blueprint to guide future investments along the entirety of the line. This work is a clear example of how the MTA is taking a bold, forward-looking approach to tackle the impacts of climate change, and addresses climate vulnerability findings from the 2024 MTA Climate Resilience Roadmap , as well as state of good repair findings from the 2025-2044 Twenty-Year Needs Assessment .     The design phase of the project will be a joint venture between STV and WSP. Construction is expected to begin in 2029.     Located right on banks of the Hudson River, Metro-North’s Hudson Line is vulnerable to flooding from stormwater run-off during extreme rain and coastal flooding – both of which are heightened by climate change. The segment between Spuyten Duyvil and Hastings-on-Hudson has experienced numerous recent floods and mudslides given its unique location between the Hudson River on the west and several steep slopes on the east, causing service disruptions on a portion of the line used by 25,000 Metro-North riders each weekday, along with Amtrak and freight rail.     The project is part of a broader effort to fortify the Hudson line. After Superstorm Sandy, the MTA completed more than $400 million of work to make the Hudson Line more resilient by improving power, communications, and signals systems along a 30-mile portion of the line from the Bronx to Croton-Harmon. The MTA is also in the midst of implementing a project to stabilize vulnerable, steep slopes and improve stormwater infrastructure on a portion of the Hudson Line between Glenwood and Greystone station, thanks to $20 million in the FY 2025 state budget from Senate Majority Leader Andrea Stewart-Cousins. This project is currently in design.     New York State Senate Majority Leader Andrea Stewart-Cousins said , “This investment in the Hudson Line is a crucial step in safeguarding our commuter network and protecting the communities that rely on it and builds on the previous funding I helped secure for this critical line. By strengthening our infrastructure, we are addressing residents’ immediate concerns and ensuring a long-term, resilient foundation for future generations. I want to thank the Governor, my colleagues in the Legislature, the MTA and the many residents that live along this line that advocated for this funding.”     Village of Hastings-on-Hudson Mayor Thomas Drake said , “On behalf of the Village of Hastings-on-Hudson, I thank Governor Hochul for moving this critical project forward. The $19.7 million design award is an important step in protecting the Hudson Line from stormwater runoff, tidal flooding and extreme weather. The planned improvements to drainage, slopes, retaining walls and shoreline structures will strengthen this vital rail corridor and help protect reliable service for the thousands of riders who depend on it every day. We appreciate the Governor’s leadership and partnership in building a more resilient Hudson Valley.”  MTA Press Release Metro-North Railroad Construction & Development

title: MTA Announces Opening of Photography Exhibit Showcasing the Behind the Scenes Work that Keeps Transit System Moving

blocks.text: In Service: MTA Photographs by Christopher Payne Gives Unprecedented Access to MTA Maintenance Shops and Manufacturing Plants Across the Country
50 Images to be Displayed in All 52 Decommissioned Advertising Lightboxes at Five Major Hubs; First Lightbox Takeover in MTA Arts and Design History
Project Pays Tribute to Unsung Workers and Highlights Investments Made Possible by Capital Plans; Caps MTA Arts and Design’s Year-Long 40th Anniversary Celebration
View Photos and Video of Press Conference

The Metropolitan Transportation Authority (MTA) today announced the opening of In Service: MTA Photographs by Christopher Payne, a series of 50 photographs giving riders a rare all-access look inside the maintenance shops and industrial facilities to showcase the people that help keep subways, buses, commuter railroads, bridges and tunnels running. Payne shot at 13 MTA facilities and manufacturing plants in four states, with a special focus on capturing the behind-the-scenes infrastructure work and specialized skills required to build and maintain the machines that move New York.    “Nobody throws a ribbon-cutting to celebrate routine maintenance, but it’s what enables the MTA to move 6.5 million people every day,” said MTA Chair and CEO Janno Lieber . “Christopher Payne went into our workshops and came out with photographs that shine a light on the unsung heroes of your morning commute.”    “The images reveal the scale, craft, and complexity behind an experience that, for millions of New Yorkers is simply part of the day's routine,” said MTA Arts and Design Director Tina Vaz . “Yet the effort required to sustain the nation's largest transit system is anything but routine. It depends on skilled welders, machinists, electricians, inspectors, assemblers, professionals whose expertise ensures that seven million riders can rely on us every day.”     “With these pictures, I'm hoping that people will appreciate the work that goes into making the system and also the care and how much beauty there is, and how much design is involved in the creation of the subway cars and the buses and the locomotives,” said photographer Christopher Payne . “I also want people to appreciate the people who do the work.”     Payne photographed daily maintenance work at each of the agency’s divisions — New York City Transit, MTA Bus, Long Island Rail Road, Metro-North Railroad, and Bridges & Tunnels, depicting both the people and the machines they build and maintain. He also travelled across the county to document the construction of rolling stock, made possible by past and present capital plans, before it reaches the system. This included Kawasaki’s R211 subway car assembly sites in Yonkers, New York and Lincoln, Nebraska; New Flyer’s articulated bus production in St. Cloud, Minnesota, and Jamestown, New York; and Siemens’ locomotive facility in Sacramento, California.    For nearly four decades, MTA Arts & Design has converted decommissioned advertising lightboxes into photo galleries, with one artist’s work displayed in one station. The photographs in the In Service series will be displayed in all 52 lightboxes at five major transportation hubs for the next six months – the first artist lightbox takeover in MTA Arts and Design’s 40-year history.     The stations are:   • 42 St-Bryant Park (           ) —7 lightboxes  • Atlantic Av-Barclays Ctr (                   ) — 8 lightboxes  • Bowling Green (     ) — 7 lightboxes  • Grand Central Terminal, Dining Concourse — 20 lightboxes  • Grand Central Madison — 10 lightboxes    In Service builds on Payne’s long-standing fascination with industrial manufacturing and the hidden infrastructure that powers the MTA system. The project is inspired by Payne’s MTA Overhaul Shops series, which was shot at the 207 St and Coney Island Overhaul Shops and was featured in a 2024 New York Times story on subway car repair. Ten photographs from that series anchor the exhibition; an additional 40 images were commissioned by MTA Arts & Design and produced between May and August 2026.    The exhibit honors the past 40 years of the MTA Arts and Design program while pointing to the ambitions of its next chapter. Looking ahead, riders can expect continued large-scale presentations across the program’s areas including photography, digital art, graphic art, music, and more.      About MTA Arts & Design  Since 1985, MTA Arts & Design has delivered innovative arts programming throughout New York’s transit system. Over four decades, Arts & Design has built a collection of award-winning art that reflects the diversity of the New York City region and makes travel a more engaging experience for millions of riders every day. The program has commissioned more than 400 permanent artworks and activated subway and railroad stations, train cars, and bus depots with MTA Music performances, Poetry in Motion, posters, photography, digital art, and special events.    About Christopher Payne   Christopher Payne specializes in architectural photography and the large format documentation of America's industrial heritage. Trained as an architect, he is fascinated by design, assembly, and the built form. Payne’s photographs invoke the former grandeur of the site over different seasons, capturing hints of buried streets and infrastructure now reclaimed by nature, while also providing a unique glimpse into a city’s future without people. Payne has been awarded grants from the Graham Foundation, the New York State Council on the Arts, and the New York Foundation for the Arts. His work has been featured in publications around the world and several times in special presentations by the New York Times Magazine.  Press Release

title: MTA to Issue Fines to Motorists Who Speed Through Work Zones Starting Sept. 22

blocks.text: Program Designed to Protect Road Workers and Motorists to Issue Fines to Drivers Speeding in Construction Zones Signed Into Law in 2021 by Gov. Kathy Hochul for State Highways; Expanded by State Legislature in 2025 to Include MTA Bridges and Tunnels

The Metropolitan Transportation Authority (MTA) today announced that it will begin issuing fines for speeding in work zones starting on Sept. 22.  The Automated Work Zone Safety Enforcement went into effect on June 30 and more than 15,780 warning notices have been issued since then.  The Authority activated speed cameras at operational construction zones on MTA vehicular bridges and tunnels in June as part of the Automated Work Zone Speed Enforcement Program. Building on programs already in place on state highways, the program is designed to reduce traffic accidents and road worker fatalities. Starting Sept. 22, motorists who are recorded driving more than 10 miles per hour above the posted speed limit will be subject to a fine.  Work zone speed cameras were originally authorized in 2021 by Governor Kathy Hochul to cover work zones on state highways. The program was expanded in 2025 by Governor Hochul and the New York State legislature to include MTA Bridges and Tunnels, which operates and maintains nine facilities in the five boroughs:

items: Bronx-Whitestone Bridge
Cross Bay Veterans Memorial Bridge
Henry Hudson Bridge
Hugh L. Carey Tunnel
Marine Parkway-Gil Hodges Memorial Bridge
Queens Midtown Tunnel
Robert F. Kennedy Bridge
Throgs Neck Bridge
Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge

blocks.text: The first phase, which began on June 30, issued written warnings to drivers that were caught speeding in work zones. In the second phase, which will begin on Tuesday, Sept. 22, fines will be issued. Since the program began, the speed cameras have been deployed  in 200 work zones and more than 33,000 vehicles were captured exceeding the speed limit by more than 10 miles per hour. In some instances, drivers were recorded going as fast as 111 miles per hour in a 45 miles per hour work zone and 109 miles per hour in a 35 miles per hour work zone. On average, vehicles were traveling 14.5 miles per hour over the posted speed limits in those work zones.  Violations start at $50 for the first offense and $75 for the second offense, if within 18 months of the first violation. Drivers with three or more violations will be fined $100 for each subsequent offense, if within 18 months of the first violation. These fines are subject to additional late fees. All violations are validated by a certified technician before they are issued. Because these are considered non-moving infractions, they will not appear on driving records nor be reported to insurance providers. Fines can be paid online, via mobile app, by mail, or in person at the NYC Department of Finance Business Centers.      An unmarked vehicle equipped with radar and camera equipment is stationed in active work zones and will operate during work hours. There will be signs alerting drivers to the presence of cameras posted ahead of these active construction sites.    Almost 900 fatalities and 40,000 injuries occurred in U.S. work zones in 2023. The program has proven successful on New York State Department of Transportation roads and the New York State Thruway, with a majority of road workers reporting they feel safer working in zones where the program is enforced.   Press Release Bridges and Tunnels

title: MTA Unveils Accessibility Upgrades at 149 St–Hostos Station

blocks.text: Three New Elevators Make Station Fully Accessible; Project Restores Historic 120-Year-Old Headhouse
Innovative Bundling of Accessibility Projects Saves Taxpayers Millions
See Photos of Station Upgrades

The Metropolitan Transportation Authority (MTA) today announced the opening of three new elevators at the 149 St–Hostos         subway station, making the station fully accessible. One three-stop elevator connects the street, upper platform and lower mezzanine, while two additional elevators provide connections to the lower platform. The station’s name recognizes nearby Hostos Community College and its importance to the South Bronx community and the City University of New York (CUNY) system.     “This station was built over 100 years ago, when accessibility wasn’t the priority it is today,” said MTA Chair and CEO Janno Lieber . “Thanks to past and present supporters in Washington, everyone in the Bronx – seniors, people with mobility issues, parents with strollers, and more – can now take advantage of our amazing subway system.”     "Bronx riders have another fully accessible station to celebrate with the addition of 149 St-Hostos to the fast-growing list of accessible subway stations," said MTA Construction & Development President Jamie Torres-Springer. “This marks eight subway stations made accessible this year alone, and with more than 30 others in construction across the system, we’re delivering real progress for New Yorkers who depend on accessible transit every day.”    “Subway stations serve as important landmarks and with Hostos Community College students, faculty and staff utilizing this station every day, we appreciate the opportunity to provide additional wayfinding for this community with a new name and signage,” said NYC Transit President Demetrius Crichlow. “And with new accessibility upgrades, even more New Yorkers can more easily and efficiently travel to this vibrant neighborhood.”    “Installing elevators at the 149 St–Hostos station removes barriers and creates a smoother trip for everyone who depends on this critical transfer hub,” said MTA Chief Accessibility Officer Quemuel Arroyo . “With step-free access to every level and seamless connections to the      and     trains, we're making the subway system more accessible, more equitable and more welcoming for all New Yorkers.”    In addition to the three new elevators, crews installed two new mezzanine-to-platform stairways to improve customer circulation, a new fare control area, energy-efficient LED lighting, new station artwork, new fire and public address systems, and additional security cameras. Crews also fully restored the station’s 120-year-old headhouse, which is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.     The accessibility upgrades at the 149 St-Hostos         station, which has 9,000 daily riders, were bundled with accessibility upgrades at the Tremont Av B/D station . That project included the installation of three new elevators—one connecting the street and mezzanine and two connecting the mezzanine and platforms—as well as two reconstructed and relocated staircases and new ADA platform edges. Bundling accessibility projects allows the MTA to deliver improvements better, faster and cheaper while saving taxpayers millions of dollars.    The design-build team for the 149 St–Hostos station upgrades is Tully Construction Corp and STV. The elevator manufacturer and installer is Mid-American.    There are now 163 fully accessible stations across the MTA system, 48 of which have been completed since 2020. The MTA is investing nearly $7.1 billion in station accessibility through its 2025–2029 Capital Plan to make 60 additional stations ADA accessible and modernize 45 subway elevators. This long-term commitment to systemwide accessibility puts the MTA on track to meet its goal of making 95 percent of the system accessible by 2055.    “I am proud to celebrate the opening of three new elevators at 149 Street-Hostos, a transfer hub that thousands of Bronx residents rely on every day,” said Representative Ritchie Torres .  “For too long, this station was out of reach for anyone who couldn't climb multiple flights of stairs, and now seniors, parents with strollers, and people with disabilities can finally move through it with dignity. Renaming the station for Hostos Community College also reflects a South Bronx institution that has shaped this neighborhood for decades. I am grateful to Governor Hochul for signing the legislation that made this renaming possible, and to the MTA for delivering these accessibility upgrades efficiently and saving taxpayers money in the process. I will keep pushing for the federal investment that makes progress like this possible across our subway system.”    “The accessibility upgrades at the 149th St Station will vastly improve the commuter experience for Hostos students and faculty, South Bronx residents, and many others who use this station regularly,” said State Senator José M. Serrano . “For a city that relies on public transportation, increasing transportation options for mobility-impaired New Yorkers allows everyone to utilize the system how it is intended. As the Senator representing the South Bronx, I was proud to sponsor the legislation to rename the station “149th Street-Hostos Station” in recognition of the contributions the school brings to the neighborhood, and support the accessibility upgrades. I am grateful to the MTA and everyone involved in this important project for improving accessibility and making it easier for residents to travel throughout the 29th Senate District.”     “When I introduced the legislation to rename this station for Hostos Community College, it was about making sure one of the South Bronx’s most important institutions had the recognition it deserves,” said Assembly Member Amanda N. Septimo . “Hostos has opened doors of opportunity for generations of Bronx students and families, and now its name will welcome New Yorkers every day at the gateway to its campus. Just as important, these accessibility improvements are long overdue. For far too long, seniors, people with disabilities, parents with strollers and countless Bronx riders have had to navigate a major transit hub that simply was not built to serve everyone. Today, we are finally changing that. With new elevators, a fully accessible station and better connections to the       and     trains, we are honoring an institution that defines the South Bronx while delivering the investment and accessibility our community has deserved for generations.”      “I’m thrilled to see much needed upgrades to this key subway station in the South Bronx,” said Council Member Justin E. Sanchez . “149 St-Hostos is my local stop and I know just how impactful these upgrades will be. So often I’m getting on and off the train with people with walkers, in wheelchairs, and who take a while to get down the stairs. This investment is for them and to show all South Bronx residents that we matter. This station is the gateway to the Bronx. These upgrades are going to connect us even further with the rest of the city and continue to make the South Bronx more welcoming to new residents and visitors alike.”    “The opening of the three new elevators at the 149th Street-Hostos Station brings us one step closer to achieving transit equity for commuters who depend on our subway system to move through our borough,” said Bronx Borough President Vanessa L. Gibson . “Making our subway stations more accessible is essential to ensuring that anyone who uses our city's transportation system can do so without barriers. By improving station design and adding more elevators we create a transit network that truly serves all New Yorkers. I want to thank the MTA and New York City Transit for their continued work upgrading our subway stations and commitment to ensuring our transit hubs are fully modernized.”     “We are delighted and grateful to finally have the 149 St subway station bear the name of Hostos Community College,” said CUNY Hostos Community College President Daisy Cocco De Filippis, Ph.D . “Plus, we now also have at our door the beautiful new entrance with the historic facade and a new elevator making the trains accessible to everyone. Since the 1960s, Hostos has been making higher education accessible to all, so this is a wonderful combination of vital resources for the community. We are also proud that our namesake, Eugenio María De Hostos, and his powerful advocacy for equity and opportunity, now is also honored by the city at this dynamic and thriving corner of the South Bronx.”     Press Release

title: MTA Celebrates Reopening of Tracks Raw Bar & Grill at Original Penn Station Location

blocks.text: Tracks’ Opening Continues Retail Resurgence at Penn Station Following MTA’s Reconstruction of LIRR Concourse to Create Brighter and More Spacious Passenger Areas View Video and Photos of News Conference and Restaurant
View Video of Reverend Brian Jordan Blessing the Beer Taps at Tracks’ Reopening

The Metropolitan Transportation Authority (MTA) today celebrated the reopening of Tracks Raw Bar & Grill at its original long-time location on the Long Island Rail Road (LIRR) Concourse of Penn Station. Tracks relocated in 2019 when the MTA began reconstruction of Penn Station’s Long Island Rail Road concourse, which has raised the height of the ceilings and widened the passenger areas, creating a space that resulted in dramatic improvements to customer satisfaction with Penn Station. Tracks Raw Bar & Grill has been completely renovated and upgraded, and has returned to its original location, in a corner of the LIRR concourse, behind the iconic escalator leading out to Seventh Av & 33rd St, next to Dunkin’ and Tracks 18 and 19. “LIRR and subway riders rejoice at Tracks’ return to its original Penn Station location,” said MTA Chair and CEO Janno Lieber . “After seven years above ground, the legendary tavern is coming back to a totally transformed LIRR corridor that’s achieved customer satisfaction records, and with every passing month, setting new ridership milestones.” “With its connection to LIRR history, Tracks resonates with many of our customers,” said Long Island Rail Road President Rob Free . “It’s easy to see how it became a crowd favorite, bringing people together from all walks of life who had something in common – the railroad – which I’m proud to say is seeing the strongest ridership since COVID and a 95.6% on-time performance rate.” “I want to thank the MTA, Vornado, the entire Long Island Rail Road team, and the many hardworking construction workers and skilled tradespeople who rebuilt this beautiful concourse and helped bring Tracks home,” said Tracks Raw Bar & Grill Owner Bruce Caulfield . “Most importantly, I want to thank the generations of loyal LIRR commuters, railroad employees and Penn Station visitors who have supported us over the years. We are thrilled to welcome everyone back to our original location.” “It's wonderful to welcome Bruce and Tracks back to their old location,” said 34th Street Partnership President Dan Biederman . “Bruce showed faith in our neighborhood by moving temporarily to 31st St, and his loyal following will no doubt enjoy another great, busy MSG season in the vibrant PENN DISTRICT from his beautiful new home." "Generations of New Yorkers made memories at Tracks Raw Bar & Grill in Penn Station until 2019," said Representative Jerry Nadler . "It was an ideal spot to spend time with loved ones before a Knicks or Rangers game at Madison Square Garden or simply grab a quick bite before boarding the LIRR. Tracks welcomed and fed New Yorkers for years, and I am grateful to Vornado and the MTA for bringing it back to its original location in Penn Station so many more New Yorkers can enjoy the Tracks experience.” “I know how hard it is to operate a business at a bar in New York City and to have life change around you while trying to make it here in this very large, expensive city,” said Assembly Member Keith Powers . “This is great news because we are standing in a modern Penn Station, bringing back a business, which was iconic and really does feel like home for so many people. And if you look inside, you can see how many New Yorkers are happy to be here, and back in the modern Penn Station with Tracks back.” “For the last seven years, I've gone to Tracks to get soup for lunch every day, right across the street – some of the best in town, and it was not uncommon to have Bruce ladling the soup into the bowl,” said NYC Council Member Carl Wilson . “I think that goes to speak to the small business feel and the personal touch that Bruce gives here at Tracks and why it is such a landmark, and such a wonderful place for people to gather. Small businesses like that are really the heartbeat of our community, and a place where we all come together and foster that community, and that is really powerful.” “Tracks has been a beloved Penn Station institution for more than two decades, and its return is wonderful news for commuters, visitors and the entire Manhattan community,” said Manhattan Borough President Brad Hoylman-Sigal. “This reopening celebrates a successful local small business while adding new energy to the beautifully transformed LIRR concourse.” Tracks first opened in 2003 and is one of the oldest operating establishments in Penn Station. It’s known for its railroad theme with murals and vintage photographs that detail the history of the LIRR. The restaurant became a popular spot for commuters, railroad employees and visitors to Penn Station. This popularity led Tracks to open a second location in Grand Central Madison in September 2025, becoming the first establishment to open in the new eastern terminal. Complementing Tracks’ return, is LIRR ridership. Post Labor Day ridership continues to show strong and consistent growth. On Wednesday, Sept. 9, the LIRR set a new record for weekday ridership, carrying 321,497 riders – surpassed only by June 18’s ridership for the Knicks Championship Parade with 369,482 riders. This strong ridership also means more customers through Penn Station, with approximately 150,000 LIRR riders passing through the station on an average weekday. The modernized LIRR concourse offers a wide variety of dining and retail options, from quick-service restaurants, cafes, to convenience stores and grab-and-go locations. With nearly all of the retail space now occupied, customers have plenty of choices to enjoy in a brighter, more modern and welcoming space. Press Release Long Island Rail Road

title: Mass Transit is the Best Way to Travel During the United Nations General Assembly

blocks.text: Subways Run Every 2-5 Minutes During Rush Hours Buses May be Delayed and/or Rerouted Due to Enhanced Security Measures and Road Closures Service Information Available on the MTA Website, App, Email and Text Alerts The Metropolitan Transportation Authority (MTA) today is informing customers to skip the traffic gridlock and take mass transit while the United Nations’ 81st session of the General Assembly takes place. The United Nations is hosting leaders from 193 member states to address the world’s most pressing issues. High-level general debates open on Tuesday, Sept. 22, and will run through Monday, Sept. 28. New York City Transit (NYCT) customers should know that the fastest and most convenient way to get around town is by hopping on the subway.  Along the East Side of Manhattan,      trains run every four minutes during the day and every two and a half to three minutes during rush hours and take 15 minutes to travel between 59 St and Wall St. During rush hour, the trains run every three minutes along the East Side of Manhattan.  Trains on the    line run every four to five and a half minutes during the day and every two to two and a half minutes during rush hours and take just nine minutes to travel between Times Sq-42 St and Long Island City’s Vernon Blvd-Jackson Av Station. Across 53 St, trains on the          lines run every three to four minutes during the day and every two to three minutes during rush hour and take just 17 minutes to travel between Forest Hills and Lexington Ave.  Trains on the         lines run every four minutes during the day and every three and a half to four and a half minutes during rush hour and take just eight minutes to travel between 34 St-Herald Sq and Canal St.  Due to increased security and resulting traffic congestion, customers are advised of multiple bus route service changes and potential delays to Paratransit trips. Customers traveling in the area via bus and Access-A-Ride should allow for additional travel time to get to and from their destinations and check the MTA app for the latest service updates. Subway and bus customers are encouraged to use the MTA’s contactless fare payment system by tapping their credit or debit card, smartphone, wearable device, or OMNY card at fare arrays and aboard buses for a streamlined travel experience.  Customers can also take advantage of Long Island Rail Road service to Grand Central Madison and Metro-North Railroad service to Grand Central Terminal. On-time performance for the Long Island Rail Road has reached 97% in 2026 while Metro-North Railroad is at 98%.  Since the launch of Congestion Relief, more than 27 million fewer vehicles entered the Congestion Relief Zone in its first year in 2025. Daily entries were down more than 73,000 or 11% on average. Traffic speeds within the zone were up 4.3% in 2025 compared to 2024, while morning rush-hour speeds at crossings improved 23% and local bus speeds rose 2 to 3% on average.  Ways to Stay Informed   The MTA offers customers a variety of ways to receive real-time and planned service change information, as well as 24/7 customer support in their native language.  mta.info  – The definitive source for real-time arrival information and service change information for each line or route in the MTA system. Customers can find current statuses on mta.info and upcoming planned service changes using the lookup tool at mta.info/alerts.    MTA app  – Customers who use the comprehensive MTA app will see real-time train, bus and rail arrival times, and can chat with the customer care team all in one place. The app is available in the Apple Store and in Google Play. TrainTime app – The MTA’s TrainTime app is the essential companion to navigating the commuter rail system. Customers can plan their trip, purchase tickets, check train status, and chat with customer service, all in one app. The app is available in the Apple Store and in Google Play.   Email & Text Alerts  – Customers can sign up for email and SMS alerts tailored to their specific commutes and travel times. They can also sign up for MTA newsletters like The Weekender, a weekly newsletter that covers major weekend planned service changes. Customers can sign up  here .    511 – Customers who prefer to contact the MTA by telephone, information is available by dialing 511. Those who are deaf or hard of hearing can use their preferred service provider for the free 711 relay to reach the MTA at 511.   MTA

blocks.text: Major Reductions to Train Service Between Stamford and New Haven Planned for Select Weekends from Now Through November 1
Customers Encouraged to Seek Alternate Forms of Transportation; Local Metro-North Service Between Grand Central and Stamford Not Affected
New Bridge Will Improve Service and Reliability for Hundreds of Thousands of Daily Customers

The Metropolitan Transportation Authority (MTA) today reminds Metro-North Railroad customers of upcoming weekend service changes that support critical high tower cable removal at the WALK Bridge Replacement Project in Norwalk, Connecticut. During five select weekends from now until November 1, Metro-North trains will run on modified schedules with reduced service between New Haven and Grand Central Terminal along the New Haven Line.     During weekend construction periods, Metro-North schedules will be adjusted across the New Haven Line between New York, Stamford, and New Haven. Metro-North local service on the western half of the line between Grand Central and Stamford, including all stations in Westchester County and Greenwich, will not be affected except for a schedule adjustment to one Saturday-only morning train. Customers are advised to check schedules prior to travel during affected weekends.    This work is a major milestone in the WALK Bridge Replacement Program and is essential to maintaining long-term reliability along the Northeast Corridor.  The new bridge will improve reliability, reduce service disruptions, and enhance rail operations for decades to come. These schedule modifications are necessary to allow crews to safely remove two 234-foot-tall utility towers and overhead wire systems on the existing 130-year-old WALK Bridge, which crosses the Norwalk River in Norwalk, CT.     Train Service Changes Planned During WALK Bridge Construction Weekends    To support critical construction activities for the WALK Bridge Program this fall, Metro-North Railroad will operate a modified train service on select weekends while working to maximize travel options and available capacity for customers.    During each affected weekend, Metro-North service will include:

items: Grand Central-New Haven trains will run on reduced frequencies and capacities.
A shuttle train service will operate between New Haven and Bridgeport.
Main-line trains operate between Grand Central Terminal and South Norwalk, with express service between Grand Central Terminal and Stamford and local service between Stamford and South Norwalk.

blocks.text: Customers should expect significantly reduced seating capacity and potential crowding, with approximately 55% fewer seats available compared with a typical weekend schedule.    Customers should be aware of three critical construction weekends:     Sept. 19-20: Wire Demolition Work    The weekend of Sept. 19-20 will see the most significant adjustments to New Haven Line schedules during the WALK Bridge reconstruction project because of the demolition of the legacy catenary wire infrastructure that powers the electric trains. A diesel-powered service plan will be implemented for trains between GCT and New Haven during wire-demolition activities. Trains will operate approximately every 90 minutes through the work zone.    Because of the wire-demolition activities, diesel equipment will be assigned to the New Haven Line for these weekends to operate through trains between New Haven and Grand Central. The diesel-hauled trains have less capacity than the normal electric trains, so customers should expect crowding. Customers traveling to and from New York City are encouraged to use the high-capacity parking garages at Stamford and South Norwalk to ride the more frequent trains between those stations.     Oct. 10-11 and Oct. 17-18: High Tower Work    During high tower construction activities on these weekends, electric train service will continue to operate through the WALK Bridge reconstruction zone during scheduled work windows. Approximately five trains are planned to operate during each work window to maximize customer travel opportunities, but there will be approximately 30% fewer seats available compared with a typical weekend schedule.    Metro-North will issue special schedules for the October work weekends in late September. Passengers are encouraged to review schedules before traveling and allow additional time for their trip during these construction weekends.    Stay informed:    The construction schedule is subject to change.     Customers are encouraged to review train schedules and service information using the MTA TrainTime and Amtrak apps before traveling:

title: MTA is the Best Way to Get to Belmont Park as the Historic Racetrack Reopens

blocks.text: Belmont Park Reopens Friday, Sept. 18, Following Three-Year Redevelopment
LIRR to Add 17 Trains for Friday’s Reopening; Railroad Provides 90 Trains Each Weekday and 159 Each Weekend Day to Elmont-UBS Arena Station
NYRA to Provide Shuttle Service from Station to Racetrack During Race Days

The Metropolitan Transportation Authority (MTA) and the New York Racing Association, Inc. (NYRA) today encouraged racing fans to take the train to Belmont Park starting Friday, Sept. 18, when the historic racetrack reopens following a three-year redevelopment.  Located along the Long Island Rail Road’s Main Line, Elmont-UBS Arena Station will serve as the primary transit gateway to the racetrack throughout the 2026 fall meet. NYRA will provide continuous shuttle service from the station platform directly to the racetrack grounds during racing hours. Belmont Park is also a short walk from the station.  The LIRR will add 17 trains serving Elmont-UBS Arena Station this Friday for the racetrack’s reopening. As part of its regular schedule, the railroad provides 90 trains to the station each weekday and 159 each weekend day, offering racing fans frequent and convenient service to Belmont Park from New York City and communities across Long Island. The completion of the Main Line Third Track provides the operational flexibility for trains traveling in both directions to serve the station while maintaining reliable service across the railroad.  “When we opened Elmont-UBS Arena Station, we knew customers would take full advantage of the reliability and high level of service that the Long Island Rail Road provides,”  said LIRR President Rob Free . “Millions of people have taken the Long Island Rail Road to attend various events at the park, giving fans from Long Island and across New York City a convenient and great customer experience.”  “Parking might be at a premium, but getting to Belmont Park doesn’t have to be,”  said MTA Chief Customer Officer Shanifah Rieara . “The LIRR gets you steps from the track, and if the subway or bus is closer, you have options too. Use the MTA app and TrainTime to plan the most convenient and affordable way to get to the races.”  “We are thrilled to unveil a new and reimagined Belmont Park on September 18 and encourage fans to ride the LIRR to the races this fall,”  said David O’Rourke, NYRA President & CEO . “Thanks to the leadership and vision of Governor Hochul, it’s a new era for Belmont Park and world class horse racing in New York.”  Belmont Park will reopen with a three-day opening weekend from Friday, Sept. 18, through Sunday, Sept. 20. Opening Day will feature the Grade 1, $1 million Jockey Club Gold Cup, along with live entertainment and other festivities.  The 46-day fall meet will continue through Sunday, Dec. 6, with live racing generally conducted Thursday through Sunday. General admission is $7 when purchased in advance and $10 when purchased at Belmont Park on the day of the event.  Customers can plan their trips to Elmont-UBS Arena Station using the TrainTime app or at MTA.info. Tickets can be purchased through TrainTime or from ticket machines at LIRR stations. Information about the Belmont Park fall meet, admission and racing schedule is available at NYRA.com/Belmont.  Getting to Belmont by NYC Subway and Bus   Belmont Park can also be reached from New York City with a convenient trip via the subway and bus.   Race fans can ride the     to 169 St or 179 St to connect with the MTA's Q2 or Q82 bus routes service right to Belmont Park, or NICE Bus' N1, N6 or N6X bus routes, which stop on Hempstead Turnpike right in front of Belmont Park.   The fare for all buses is $3.00, but the MTA offers subway riders a free transfer on the Q2 or Q82 when they tap to ride.  Belmont Park Redevelopment Project   Following a three-year redevelopment, Belmont Park will reopen for live racing on Friday, Sept. 18. The reimagined venue features a modern grandstand, new fan amenities and hospitality offerings, and four newly constructed racing surfaces.  Admission gates will open at 11:00 a.m. daily unless otherwise noted. First post is scheduled for 1:30 p.m. on Opening Day, 12:05 p.m. on Saturdays and 1:10 p.m. on Thursdays, Fridays and Sundays throughout September. General admission on Saturday, Sept. 19, and Sunday, Sept. 20, is $10.00 and includes a commemorative program. Beginning Thursday, Sept. 24, admission is $7.00 when purchased in advance and $10.00 on the day of the event, with a complimentary program included. Press Release

blocks.text: First-Ever Veterans Recruitment Event at MTA Aimed to Attract Top Service Member Talent Across Sectors
View Photos of Information Session

The Metropolitan Transportation Authority (MTA) hosted its inaugural Veterans in Transit Career Information Session in partnership with the MTA’s Veterans Employee Resource Group (ERG) at the Authority’s headquarters located at 2 Broadway in Lower Manhattan. The event brought together military veterans, transitioning service members, and workforce development partners to learn about MTA skilled trades and operations careers, hiring pathways, qualifications, career progression and how military experience and technical skills can translate to opportunities at the MTA. More than 120 veterans registered to attend the information session, with the deadline for registration being extended to accommodate the high level of interest among the public. “The MTA is committed to recruiting the best talent from every corner of the country with technical skills across sectors, and that includes veterans,” said MTA Chief People Officer Mersida Ibric. “This event provided helpful information to veteran attendees who we hope to attract with a great career in transportation, while also advancing the Authority’s strategic mission of providing the best service possible to customers across the service area with the highest caliber talent.”  “We are so happy to be hosting the first-ever Veterans in Transit event at MTA headquarters,” said MTA Veterans Employee Resource Group (ERG) President and Director of Security Training & Development All Agency at the Office of Security Jesse DeMino . “This is a wonderful opportunity to highlight the many skills our brave service members have learned while defending our country and put them to use in keeping the New York metropolitan area moving every day.” The program included an overview of the various career opportunities and career pathways available for current and former service members at the MTA, as well as information about the hiring process and service examinations required. Attendees listened to a panel discussion hosted by MTA veteran employees and interacted with skilled trades subject matter experts. In addition, attendees were able to network with current MTA employees. Representatives from across the MTA were in attendance including MTA Headquarters, People Department, New York City Transit, Construction & Development, Long Island Rail Road, and Metro-North Railroad. The event was also held in partnership with affiliated organizations participating including the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs; New York State Department of Veterans’ Services; New York State Department of Labor; Queens Borough President’s Office; Workforce1, Upper Manhattan; New York Auto and Diesel Institute (NYADI) The College of Transport Technology; Nassau County  Board of Cooperative Educational Services (Nassau BOCES); Services for the UnderServed (SUS); Apex Technical Institute, and Grant Associates. title: ICYMI: Governor Hochul Announces MTA Advances Final Construction Contract of Second Avenue Subway Phase 2

blocks.text: Request for Qualifications for Final Contract of Subway Extension Project Issued

Fourth Contract Includes Work To Complete Station Buildouts, Ancillary Buildings, Communication Systems, 22 Elevators, 20 Escalators and Other Station Infrastructure Across Three New East Harlem Stations

Governor Hochul today announced that the Metropolitan Transportation Authority (MTA) is advancing the fourth and final construction contract for Phase 2 of the Second Avenue Subway, marking a major milestone toward completing the extension of     service to 125 St in East Harlem. Following this Request for Qualifications (RFQ), the MTA plans to issue a Request for Proposals to qualified contractors by the end of the year and anticipates selecting a contractor in mid-2027. Contract Four is the largest contract of the Second Avenue Subway Phase 2 project and includes the construction of station infrastructure, tracks, and signals for the subway expansion. Work on Contract Four will begin in 2027.  “New Yorkers have been waiting for the Second Avenue Subway for nearly a century and now, with major work underway, we are moving full speed ahead with the final contract to fully deliver this transformative new transit connection to East Harlem,” Governor Hochul said . “We fought hard to keep this project moving forward earlier this year and finally break ground on new tunnels this summer. Once this contract is completed, three beautiful and accessible new subway stations will welcome East Harlem to the subway line they have long been promised.”  With the first three contracts progressing concurrently, the project budgeted at $6.968 billion is expected to be fully completed by the fall of 2032. This project is made possible by congestion relief revenue and $3.4 billion in federal funding. Upon completion of Phase 2,     service will run north from 96 St to 125 St and Lexington Ave, an extension of approximately 1.5 miles with three new stations at 106 St, 116 St and 125 St.  MTA Chair and CEO Janno Lieber said , “Three contracts down, one to go in our quest to bring long-awaited transit justice to East Harlem. This fourth and final RFQ covers the architectural finishes and the communications and other systems in the stations – the things that riders directly experience – and we can’t wait to get started.”  MTA Construction & Development President Jamie Torres-Springer said , “The MTA has saved more than $1 billion to date by applying lessons learned from Phase 1 to Phase 2. We're bringing that same approach to this final contract to bring these stations to life better, faster, and cheaper than before and get East Harlem riders the service they’ve waited for."  In addition to providing the full systems fit-out for the three fully accessible stations at 106 St, 116 St, and 125 St, and connecting tunnel segments, this fourth contract includes work to connect the new 125 St Station to the existing 125 St 4 5 6 station, and an entrance at Park Ave, one block over, enabling convenient transfers to Metro-North’s Harlem-125 St Station and M60 Select Bus Service with service to LaGuardia Airport.  Major work in this last construction contract includes:

items: Structural work : Construction of entrance canopies, station platforms and six above-ground ancillary buildings which will house ventilation, mechanical, and electrical equipment, as well as space for possible ground floor retail and community uses.
Mechanical, electrical and plumbing work : Install HVAC, smoke management, fire protection, station and facility power, lighting, plumbing and drainage, and related systems.
Accessibility work : Install 22 elevators and 20 escalators across the three stations and facilities.
Communications and security systems work : Install public address systems, customer information screens, Help Point intercoms, Wi-Fi, radio, fire and emergency alarms, and security cameras.
Track, signal and CBTC work : Install track, third rail, traction power, wayside signal equipment, train detection, communication infrastructure throughout the stations and tunnels.
Station finishes : Install architectural finishes, station lighting, signage and wayfinding, fare arrays, customer service facilities and artwork.
Testing and commissioning work : Test, integrate and commission all systems installed.
Site restoration : Complete permanent utility connections and restore streets, sidewalks, traffic signals and other affected areas within the Phase 2 project limits.

blocks.text: Phase 2 Construction Progress  The first contract, awarded in January 2024, covers utility relocation work at the future 106 St Station. The project is currently about 60 percent complete and is expected to be finished by summer 2027. Getting ahead of utility relocation work is a major lesson learned from Phase 1.  The second contract, awarded in September 2025, includes construction of two tunnels, rehabilitation of existing tunnels, construction of the new 116 St Station box, seven shafts for future ancillary buildings and station entrances, and the structural shells for the 116 St and 125 St stations. Final design is more than 50 percent complete. The tunnel boring machine (TBM) is currently under construction, and crews are preparing the TBM launch site for excavation. Excavation of the 125 St entrance shaft has also begun. The contract is forecast to reach substantial completion in September 2029.  The third contract, awarded in April 2026, includes excavation and construction of the 106 St structural shell, tunnel connections, ancillary buildings and station entrances, as well as utility work. The contract is expected to reach substantial completion in the third quarter of 2030.  Delivering Better Transit for East Harlem  East Harlem is a historically underserved neighborhood which has one of the largest concentrations of affordable housing in the United States and where 70 percent of residents rely on transit. Phase 2 is building three new accessible stations right in the heart of the community at 106 St, 116 St, and 125 St, and will offer one-seat rides from East Harlem to the Upper East Side, West Midtown and Coney Island, shortening travel times by up to 20 minutes. The Second Avenue Subway Phase 2 project is also creating thousands of jobs, including union-wage construction jobs. A 20 percent local hiring goal for the project will generate good-paying job opportunities for hundreds of East Harlem residents.  East Harlem has long been promised a new subway connection on Second Avenue. In the 1920s, the Second System proposal, which ultimately became the IND subway system, included service on Second Avenue. In 1948, New York City voters approved bonding intended to build the Second Avenue Subway, which was ultimately left unbuilt after the start of the Korean War. In 1972, construction on the line finally commenced in East Harlem, but was later abandoned in 1975 during the city’s fiscal crisis. Sections of the tunneling constructed in the 1970s will be adapted and utilized in Phase 2, including for the 116 St station.  Senator Charles Schumer said , “I secured $3.4 billion in federal funding for the Second Avenue Subway, the largest Capital Investment Grant in history, and this final contract brings East Harlem another big step closer to transportation equity. When the work is done, more than 300,000 riders will benefit every day and I will not stop advocating for construction until the    is running to 125th Street."  Senator Kirsten Gillibrand said , “New Yorkers have waited decades for the completion of the Second Avenue Subway Extension into East Harlem. This critical infrastructure project will deliver the safe, reliable, and accessible public transportation system that our commuters and families deserve. I am proud to have secured the federal funding that is making this vital expansion to the New York City subway system possible, and I’ll continue working to bring home more federal resources to improve public transportation for all New Yorkers.”  Representative Adriano Espaillat said , "With this contract advancement, the community of East Harlem is one step closer to subway access — after nearly a century of poor connectivity with our nation's largest train system. Since my election to the U.S. Congress, I have prioritized the expansion of the Second Avenue Subway and generation of local, dignified trade jobs alongside the project. This development is another welcomed victory in our long, winding journey to deliver equitable transportation access and economic growth in El Barrio. I commend our partners, including local officials at the MTA, for their daily efforts to keep the project on time and under budget."  State Senator José Serrano said , “Second Avenue Subway Project is a critical investment in transit equity that is long overdue for residents and commuters from East Harlem and beyond. While this project is vital for our community, it has created challenges for local residents and businesses along 2nd Avenue. The final phase of this project brings us closer to overall completion, and we thank Governor Kathy Hochul, the MTA, and my colleagues in government for bringing us one step closer to delivering the safe, reliable, and accessible system that New Yorkers deserve."  State Senator Cordell Cleare said , "I welcome this milestone on behalf of our community which so richly deserves transit equity.  I truly hope that this phase of the project will empower the local community and provide a much needed suite of benefits to our entire neighborhood." New York City Council Majority Leader Shaun Abreu said , “I’m excited to see the MTA take another major step in delivering this once-in-a-generation transportation project for Upper Manhattan. This subway line will dramatically improve life uptown, from commute times to job opportunities and boosts to small businesses. Like so many others, I’m excited to see the new stations come to life, and I’m grateful for Governor Hochul and Chair Lieber’s continued leadership.”  Manhattan Borough President Brad Hoylman-Sigal said , “I’m thrilled that Governor Hochul and the MTA are moving full steam ahead on Phase Two of the Second Avenue Subway, a landmark project that East Harlem has waited far too long to see completed. Extending the Q train to 125th Street will finally bring faster, more reliable subway service to East Harlem and better connect residents to jobs, schools and the rest of our city. I’m grateful to Governor Hochul and MTA Chair Janno Lieber for continuing to prioritize this critical investment in Manhattan’s transit infrastructure. Let’s get it built. I look forward to the ribbon-cutting!”   Press Release Construction & Development

title: ICYMI: Better Buses: Governor Hochul Announces MTA Seeking Companies to Upgrade Fleet with 650 New, Alternative-Fuel Buses

blocks.text: Biggest Single Upgrade to Bus Fleet Since 2013
Upgrading Fleet Improves Service Reliability by Building on Steps Outlined in ‘Next Stop’ Bus Action Plan in Partnership with Mayor Mamdani
New Buses Will Use Compressed Natural Gas, a Cleaner, Cost-Effective Alternative to Diesel
Request for Proposal (RFP) Is Available Here ; MTA’s 2025-29 Capital Plan Is Available Here

Governor Kathy Hochul announced today the Metropolitan Transportation Authority (MTA) will be releasing a request for proposals (RFPs) from bus manufacturing companies to build 650 new buses, the biggest single upgrade to the fleet since 2013. When the full order has been completed, these new buses will represent more than 10 percent of the MTA’s bus fleet and will serve more than one million daily riders. These buses will be purchased with funding secured by Governor Hochul in the MTA’s historic 2025-29 Capital Plan and will fulfill the MTA’s commitment to modernize its bus fleet made in the Next Stop: Faster Buses, Better Service plan announced in partnership with Governor Hochul and New York City Mayor Zohran Kwame Mamdani this summer. The buses will use Compressed Natural Gas (CNG), a cheaper, greener alternative to diesel fuel. The new buses, which will replace aging CNG buses already in service, will improve fleet reliability, reduce emissions and improve air quality.  “We promised New Yorkers a historic partnership with City Hall to move buses faster and more reliably, now we are delivering by moving full speed ahead with the single largest purchase of new MTA buses in over a decade,” Governor Hochul said. “Modern, reliable buses can spend more time on the road and less time in the shop than the old vehicles they will replace, a win for riders who depend on frequent, reliable service to get around.”  Mayor Zohran Kwame Mamdani said,  “Working New Yorkers depend on our buses to get to work, get their kids to school, get home and get where they need to go. This investment will help us deliver the faster, more reliable and more affordable bus service New Yorkers deserve while modernizing our fleet and moving to cleaner, greener fuel. I’m proud to partner with Governor Hochul and the MTA to make that vision a reality and build a transit system that works for every New Yorker.”  MTA Chair and CEO Janno Lieber said, “The Governor and Mayor have been clear: better bus service can’t wait. So, while the electric bus industry continues to mature, MTA is moving forward with CNGs to further improve service for the millions of New Yorkers who ride MTA buses every day.”  MTA Chief of Rolling Stock Jessie Lazarus said, “These 650 Compressed Natural Gas buses are a core part of our strategy to deliver faster, greener, more cost-efficient service to the millions of daily customers who depend on our bus service. Through large order sizes like this one, plus the potential for multiple awards, we are leveraging the MTA’s multibillion dollar commitment to the future of our transit system to get as many new buses into service as soon as possible.”  New York City Transit President Demetrius Crichlow said, “Modern buses make a big difference on our ability to deliver efficient, reliable and safe service for the millions of daily customers who ride the system every day. We’re continuing to forward our goal of a greener fleet and a more resilient transit system for future generations while ensuring we maintain the service New Yorkers deserve.”  State Senator Jeremy Cooney said, “New York moves fast — and our public transportation should too. This investment delivers cheaper, greener transit options and puts riders and bus drivers first. I’m grateful for Governor Hochul’s continued support in ensuring a strong transportation network throughout the state.”  City Council Majority Leader Shaun Abreu said, “650 new buses will help ensure that the MTA’s fleet can meet the challenge of delivering faster and more reliable service for New Yorkers. The investment supports a greener future while putting riders first, and I’m grateful for Governor Hochul and Chair Lieber’s leadership on the critical upgrade.”  In July, the MTA stood with Governor Hochul and Mayor Mamdani to release “ Next Stop: Faster Buses, Better Service ,” an initiative to increase speeds and improve service. Since then, 41 new buses have entered service to replace the oldest buses with an average age of 18 years — the oldest was 21 years old — well beyond their useful life.  The MTA is committed to gradually replacing older diesel buses with more environmentally-friendly vehicles in a manner that maintains safe, reliable, and affordable bus service for the millions of daily riders. As part of that strategy, 30 percent of standard bus purchases in this Capital Plan are expected to be CNG buses. This Capital Plan also provides for the purchase of 500 zero-emission buses and the installation of charging infrastructure at bus depots, with a focus on bus depots in communities disproportionately affected by poor air quality.  100 percent of the natural gas used to fuel CNG buses is offset by renewable natural gas (RNG), which is made using methane captured from organic sources including landfills and farms and thus dramatically reduces lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions. CNG buses are also quieter, reducing noise pollution. Using RNG also protects the Authority from diesel price swings, saving taxpayers money. In addition, CNG buses require less maintenance and are generally more reliable compared to diesel buses.  This RFP is part of the MTA’s new Rolling Stock Program, which approaches rolling stock procurement contracts differently by encouraging innovation by giving manufacturers greater flexibility to propose new ideas. This results in a streamlined contract that will ensure the Authority can deliver quality cars and buses in a timely manner, while giving riders the best value for their tax dollars.  Proposals are due October 19, 2026.  Press Release

title: Better Buses: MTA Announces Automated Camera Enforcement Expanding to Two Bus Routes in Queens

blocks.text: Q25 and Q63/Q66 to Become ACE Equipped
60-Day Warning Period Begins Monday, Sept. 14
19 Routes of 25 Activated in 2026 as Part of Fast Buses Plan
ACE Program Benefits More Than One Million Riders on 73 Routes

The Metropolitan Transportation Authority (MTA) today announced two additional bus routes will now be equipped with Automated Camera Enforcement (ACE). The 60-day warning period on the Q25 and Q63/Q66 bus routes in Queens will begin on Monday, Sept 14. The goal of the program is to improve bus service by enhancing compliance with existing traffic rules. Vehicles improperly using busways and bus lanes, blocking bus stops, or illegally double parked will receive warning notices in the mail for an initial period of 60 days. Once the warning period ends, summonses will start at $50 for the first offense and escalate to $250 for repeat violators. As outlined in the Next Stop: Fast Buses, Better Service plan , the MTA is committed to getting buses running faster and more reliably for riders. This comprehensive bus action plan builds on the previous success of the ACE program by promising to expand ACE to an additional 25 routes in 2026 in addition to working with City partners to enhance bus lane enforcement. The Q25 and Q63/Q66 will bring the total numbers of routes to go live this year to 19. With the addition of these routes, ACE is now enforced on a total of 73 routes. More than 2,000 buses, or one third of the entire bus fleet, are now ACE equipped, covering approximately 825 route miles and benefiting over one million riders on an average weekday. The Q25 and Q63/Q66 routes serve a combined weekday ridership of approximately 47,700 riders. ACE allows buses to run faster, safer, and more reliably. When combined with dedicated bus lanes and street upgrades, the ACE program has helped to improve bus speeds across the full length of ACE-enabled routes, with some segments on ACE routes achieving gains of nearly 30%. The ACE program is administered in partnership with the New York City Department of Transportation (NYCDOT) and the New York City Department of Finance (NYCDOF). Once violations are captured by cameras on multiple buses, the resulting video, images, license plate information, location, and time stamp details are then securely transmitted to NYCDOT for review by City employees and processing thereafter. Since its launch in June 2024, ACE has rapidly expanded from a few select routes to a citywide initiative covering all five boroughs. The program has shown measurable success in improving bus speeds, reducing traffic accidents, and keeping bus stops clear – ensuring New Yorkers can get to where they need to go safely and on time. Each corridor with active ACE has signage indicating that those routes are camera-enforced. Details can be found at mta.info/ace .   Press Release New York City Transit MTA Bus Company

Today, the Metropolitan Transportation Authority (MTA) announced to motorists that Automated Camera Enforcement (ACE) fines will begin on additional bus routes starting Friday, Sept. 11. The goal of the program is to improve bus service by enhancing compliance with existing traffic rules. Vehicles improperly using busways and bus lanes, blocking bus stops, or illegally double parked along the B38, B103, Bx11, and Bx17 bus routes in the Bronx and Brooklyn — routes that serve tens of thousands of daily riders — will receive summonses that start at $50 and escalate to $250 for repeat violators.      As outlined in the Next Stop: Fast Buses, Better Service plan , the MTA is committed to getting buses running faster and more reliably for riders. This comprehensive bus action plan builds on the previous success of the ACE program by promising to expand ACE to an additional 25 routes in 2026 in addition to working with City partners to enhance bus lane enforcement. The four routes announced will total 17 routes to go live this year.      ACE is currently enforced on a total of 70 routes. More than 2,000 buses totaling one third of the bus fleet, are now ACE equipped covering approximately 825 route miles and benefiting over one million riders on an average weekday.      When combined with dedicated bus lanes and street upgrades, the ACE program has helped to improve bus speeds across the full length of ACE-enabled routes, with some segments on ACE routes achieving gains of nearly 30%.      The ACE program is administered in partnership with the New York City Department of Transportation (NYCDOT) and the New York City Department of Finance (NYCDOF). Once violations are captured by cameras on multiple buses, the resulting video, images, license plate information, location, and time stamp details are securely transmitted to NYCDOT for review by City employees and processing.    Since its launch in June 2024, ACE has rapidly expanded from a few select routes to a citywide initiative covering all five boroughs. The program has shown success in improving bus speeds, reducing traffic accidents, and keeping bus stops clear – ensuring New Yorkers can get to where they need to go safely and on time.     Each corridor with active ACE has signage indicating that those routes are camera-enforced. Details can be found at mta.info/ace .      Press Release

title: ICYMI: Governor Hochul Announces Interborough Express Project Design and Environmental Review Milestones

blocks.text: Draft Environmental Impact Statement (DEIS) Set To Be Released Ahead of Schedule Later This Year

Latest Station Renderings of the Interborough Express Are  Available Here ; Updated Interborough Express Website Is  Available Here

Governor Kathy Hochul today announced that the Metropolitan Transportation Authority (MTA) has made progress on the design and environmental review phase of the Interborough Express (IBX), a transformational new light rail connection between Brooklyn and Queens. To ensure complete accessibility along the entire IBX, the MTA is prioritizing significant accessibility projects at the final four non-accessible subway stations that will connect to the Interborough Express (IBX). Once complete, these upgrades will result in each of the IBX’s 18 stations being fully accessible, with connections to 17 subway lines and the Long Island Rail Road, providing accessible options at all transfer points. The IBX, currently in the design and engineering phase that Governor Hochul launched last August will offer a first-of-its-kind transit connection to historically underserved communities in Brooklyn and Queens, significantly shortening travel times for more than 900,000 residents and a projected 160,000 daily riders.     “For too many commuters, traveling between New York’s two largest boroughs can be lengthy, inconvenient and inaccessible — that’s why the IBX promises to change everything for Brooklyn and Queens, and we aren’t wasting any time advancing this transformational project,”  Governor Hochul said . “By pushing forward on design and accelerating accessibility upgrades at future subway connections, my administration is bringing all 900,000 New Yorkers who live near planned IBX line one stop closer to reduced travel times and an even more reliable public transit experience.”     The MTA is in process of delivering full ADA accessibility to three subway stations that will connect to the IBX route prior to the IBX opening. These stations are:     Broadway Junction            : Funded through the MTA’s 2020-24 Capital Plan

blocks.text: Accessibility at a fourth station, Wilson Ave    , has been expedited within the 2025-29 Capital Plan. A contract for the accessibility work at the station will be awarded by mid-2027. Wilson Ave will be the final IBX-subway transfer station to receive accessibility improvements.     In addition, all 18 new IBX stations will be designed with full accessibility, using universal design principles to maximize access and functionality for all riders. IBX stations will provide clear sightlines, tactile floor tiles leading to wide fare gates, pass-through elevators with wider cabs, level boarding throughout the platform, enhanced station lighting, digital signage along with audio announcements and wayfinding signage positioned for optimal viewing and clear delivery of information.     MTA Chair and CEO Janno Lieber said , “For decades, people have been dreaming of transit connections between Brooklyn and Queens. Under Governor Hochul's leadership, we are finally making that a reality with the IBX. And with universal accessibility, everyone is going to benefit.”     MTA Construction & Development President Jamie Torres-Springer said , “The Interborough Express will transform travel in Brooklyn and Queens, cutting commute times for more than 160,000 daily riders. From day one, we’re building accessibility into every aspect of the project—because every rider should be able to take full advantage of this new way to move across the boroughs.”     MTA Chief Accessibility Officer Quemuel Arroyo said , “By building the IBX as a fully accessible rail system, riders will be able to travel between Brooklyn and Queens faster than ever before. We’re working with community partners throughout the design process to ensure their voices are heard and needs are met.”     Assemblymember Claire Valdez said , “Mass transit should be the great equalizer: it should be affordable, reliable, and accessible. I'm thrilled that the long-awaited IBX is not only moving forward, but that existing stations are being prioritized for accessibility upgrades. The IBX is a transformative investment in public transit and in every working New Yorker's ability to get where they need to go. I'm thrilled that it will be designed for everyone.”     Governor Hochul also announced that the MTA will release the Draft Environmental Impact Statement (DEIS) for the IBX ahead of schedule in Q4 of this year. The release of the DEIS will reflect the progress being made by the IBX project team and be a significant milestone in the development of the $5.5 billion project to connect Brooklyn and Queens.     The release of the DEIS will be followed by a series of public meetings where Brooklyn and Queens residents will be able to share their thoughts on the IBX. There have been nearly 30 pop-up events held this summer with more than 7,000 local community member engagements, and approximately 140 events hosted across the entirety of the project. In the spring, the project team met with all 14 community boards that line the IBX corridor and hosted a series of public workshops to solicit input on the design featuring interactive activities from more than 425 participants and 6,000 feedback responses submitted.     About the Interborough Express (IBX)    The IBX will connect communities in Brooklyn and Queens to 17 subway lines, 51 current bus routes, the Long Island Rail Road, as well as significantly reduce travel times within and between the two boroughs. More than 160,000 riders are expected to use the line each weekday - more riders than any light rail system currently operating in the United States today. In October of 2025, the MTA awarded a contract to begin the design phase of the IBX, which is expected to take approximately two years.     The IBX will be the first new end-to-end rapid transit built entirely within New York City since the IND Crosstown Line, now called the G, which fully opened in 1937. IBX stations in Queens will be the first new transit stations built since the Archer Avenue extension of the       and     lines to Jamaica in 1988.     Funding the IBX    The current project design phase is funded mainly through $45 million secured by Governor Hochul in New York’s FY 2026 state budget and the MTA’s 2025-29 Capital Plan. The total estimated cost of the IBX project is $5.5 billion. $2.75 billion in funding for the project was approved by Governor Hochul in the MTA’s 2025-29 Capital Plan.    MTA Press Release New York City Transit Construction & Development
